questions.q: What is this lesson's SimpleGovernor contract explicitly described as?
options: A production-ready contract safe to deploy as-is
A simplified teaching example, not production code -- real DAOs should use OpenZeppelin's audited Governor + TimelockController
An exact copy of OpenZeppelin's Governor contract
A contract that requires no further security review
questions.explain: The lesson opens with an explicit disclaimer that this is a simplified teaching example missing hardening a real DAO needs, and that production DAOs should use audited OpenZeppelin contracts instead.

questions.q: In propose(), what is snapshotBlock set to, and when?
options: block.number, re-read and updated every time someone votes
A fixed value of zero for every proposal
The block at which the proposal is executed
block.number, recorded once at proposal creation and never changed again
questions.explain: snapshotBlock = block.number is set once inside propose() and stays fixed, implementing the snapshot mechanic from the voting/delegation lesson.

questions.q: In castVote(), why does the function call token.getPastVotes(msg.sender, p.snapshotBlock) instead of reading the voter's current balance?
options: So tokens acquired after the proposal was created don't count toward voting power on that proposal
Because current balances are never readable in Solidity
To make the function cheaper on gas, with no security purpose
Because snapshotBlock is always equal to the current block
questions.explain: Reading weight at the fixed snapshotBlock (rather than live) is exactly what prevents last-minute token acquisition (e.g. via flash loan) from inflating voting power.

questions.q: Which two checks does execute() perform that directly implement Lesson 24's quorum and majority rules?
options: require(block.timestamp > p.voteEnd, ...) and require(!p.executed, ...) only
There are no quorum or majority checks in execute()
require(totalVotes >= QUORUM, ...) and require(p.forVotes > p.againstVotes, ...)
A single require statement checks both at once with no separate logic
questions.explain: The quorum check verifies total participation meets QUORUM; the majority check verifies forVotes exceeds againstVotes -- both must pass for execution to proceed.

questions.q: What safeguard from Lesson 26 is explicitly missing from this contract's execute() function?
options: The ability to vote at all
A timelock delay -- execute() here fires immediately once quorum/majority pass, with no mandatory waiting period
The ability to check quorum
The ability to propose a change
questions.explain: The lesson notes that execute() has no delay between voting ending and execution succeeding -- a real DAO adds a TimelockController specifically to close that gap.
